title: Harvey Mason jr. on 2,300 New Grammy Voting Members, the Asian Pop Category Uproar & More: ‘We Want To Bring More People Into the Tent’
summary: First-round Grammy voting, which determines the nominations for 2027, opens Monday and runs through Oct. 22.
contentText:
When first-round voting for the 69th annual Grammy Awards opens on Monday (Oct. 12), a considerably larger voting body will determine the nominees than in prior years.

Related

2027 Grammy Changes: 5 New Categories, More Lenient Rules on Best New Artist Eligibility and More

Grammys’ Asian Pop Category Will Go Forward at 2027 Ceremony, Recording Academy Confirms

What Does the Big Change to the Best New Artist Grammy Mean for Nominees?

The Recording Academy has revealed details of its 2026 new member class, which includes more than 2,300 new voting members. Here’s their demographic breakdown of these new voting members: People of color: 53%; people aged 39 or under: 54%; and women: 33%.

The new member class also includes more than 800 professional members, who are non-voting.

The 69th annual Grammy Awards will be presented on Feb. 7. The show will have a new host (Trevor Noah bowed out after six years) and will air/stream on new network platforms — ABC, Disney+ and Hulu — after the show ended a 54-year run on CBS.

The Academy will present 100 awards on Feb. 7, the highest number since 2011. It added five categories in June, including one that attracted far more attention than the other four combined – best Asian pop music performance. Two of the biggest acts in Asian pop – BTS and Stray Kids – announced that they wouldn’t enter the category, not wishing to be pigeonholed. It’s fair to say the Academy did not anticipate that reaction.

Harvey Mason jr. , who has been CEO of the Recording Academy since May 2021 (following a 16-month run as interim CEO), spoke with Billboard over Zoom on Wednesday (Oct. 7) for this wide-ranging discussion.

You invited the largest new member class in your history – 4,000 people. And 3,100 people took you up on it, including 2,300 voting members. Do you anticipate continuing to add members at this pace, or can you see a day when you’ll just be maintaining?

I don’t know if it’s necessarily maintaining or trying to add at a particular pace. It’s really about trying to make sure we get the right members who are relevant and qualified to be voters in our organization. As music grows and evolves and changes, I’m sure our membership will do the same. And I would imagine it would continue to grow as music is becoming more global, as more people are making music and working in our industry, so I could see some growth, but it’s going to be driven by our efforts to try and make sure our membership is the best possible membership we can assemble.

More than half of this year’s new voting members are people of color, and more than half are people aged 39 and under. One-third are women. You’re obviously zeroing in on those three demographics. Do you have targets in mind where you’d like to wind up?

Well, first, I would say we’re not really necessarily zeroing in just on those. We’re really zeroing in on holistically making sure our membership is reflective of what’s going on in music and in the world. And so, we’re always going to continue to look at those numbers and make sure that we’re being, I guess, representative — and as things change in our industry, as genres change, as popularity of different types of music changes, we hope to mirror that. The one number that I know we have been intentionally focused on was women and people of color because we were, I think, a little bit beneath the mark where we wanted to be there, so we’re getting to a better place. There’s still work to do, and we’re going to continue to watch all those numbers.

When you say there’s still work to do, it suggests that you do have some goal in mind.

It’s just my nature, and it’s the attitude and energy of our organization, that we’re always going to continue to try and improve. I won’t say that there’s a specific number we’re trying to reach, but we do want to do better every year at making sure our membership is the right membership.

Do you also look at Grammy nominations and awards results to see how you’re doing in membership?

We do, and it’s not necessarily who’s winning or who’s losing. It’s just making sure that the genres are represented and making sure we’re having enough voters with knowledge and expertise across different types of music to represent those genres across the entire ballot.

If you were to look at results, Kendrick Lamar won record of the year the last two years, this year for a collaboration with SZA. Bad Bunny won album of the year this year. I would say the results show progress.

Yes, I am proud of the progress to this point — but as I said, we want to continue to get better and evolve and make sure we’re getting this right.

In best new artist, you’ve increased the number of times someone can be entered from three to four. Why do you think artists are taking longer to break than used to be the case?

I don’t know if it’s taking longer for them to break. But I guess we’re giving them a little bit more flexibility, so they can submit one additional time. I do think, with artists being able to release music on their own sooner, that that window is extended as far as the period of time in which they first release music to when they reach popularity. Before, you had to be signed to a label, so that took some time. And then before you could release music, you needed to get either an independent distributor or a label, so that took some time. Whereas now, as soon as you start making music, if you really wanted to, you could release [it]. So, I do think that opens up the window, and gives us the need to give somebody a little bit more space to submit an additional year.

Megan Moroney won new artist of the year at the CMA Awards two years ago. Don Toliver has had five consecutive top 10 albums on the Billboard 200 dating back to 2020. So, there are artists in the mix for best new artist this year whose “newness” is debatable. You’re being quite lenient now, allowing artists to enter four times. When you’re that lenient, doesn’t it become hard to turn anyone away — and if you say no to somebody, don’t you get calls saying “How is Artist X eligible and my artist isn’t?”

We will always get those calls, whether it’s about best new artist or another category, and that’s why I always say this is this stuff is hard, and it is subjective and I’m thankful that we have committees in place, our membership in place, professional music creators making some of these judgment calls. You know, there’s committees that listen to the screened material and decide is the prominence being reached this year or have they passed it? Or are they still building? So, there’s a lot of discretion there, but it is tough. It is subjective, and only thing I can say is we’re doing everything we can to try and get it as right as we possibly can.

It seems to me that best new artist has really evolved into best breakthrough artist – the artist that made a meaningful breakthrough in this year. You’re probably locked into the best new artist name, but am I right that that is what it is? 

There’s a couple different ways to interpret “new.” Some people interpret new as someone that they’ve just started to hear of in a big way, and some [interpret] it as somebody who’s actually just starting to make music. So it really depends on the interpretation.

So, the name is here to stay.

I won’t say “here to stay,” because we revisit so many things every year, and we’re always open for discussions. And if people who submit proposals think that there’s a name change that needs to happen, we’ll always entertain that. And that’s the cool thing about our processes. There’s nothing set in stone.
